sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that false teachers will arise within the community who 'deny the Master who bought them,' where the buying is presented as a genuine, completed transaction (drawing on Deuteronomy 32's pattern of God purchasing Israel) and the denial is a subsequent, culpable act that brings swift destruction upon themselves.
sections.relevance: The phrase 'denying the Master who bought them' directly addresses who determines salvation outcomes. The Master genuinely purchased these people -- the neutral reading emphasizes that the language 'presents it as genuine -- the Master truly purchased these people, and they truly repudiated him.' If the Master bought them and they subsequently denied him, then the human act of denial -- not a divine decree -- determined their destruction. The destruction is described as self-inflicted: 'bringing swift destruction upon themselves.' This is the author's own argument, not an aside, and it presents human agency as the determining factor in the reversal of a genuine salvific relationship.
key_phrases: denying the Master who bought them
bringing swift destruction upon themselves
the Master bought them, and they deny the Master
the buying is treated as a real, completed transaction
the denial is treated as a subsequent, culpable act

sections.section_title: Three Historical Examples of Judgment and Rescue
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that three historical precedents -- the sinning angels, Noah's flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah -- demonstrate a dual pattern: God judges the ungodly and rescues the righteous, concluding that 'the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment.'
sections.relevance: While the passage's primary function is to establish God's competence in judgment and rescue, the moral categories it uses are behavioral, not decretal. The angels 'sinned'; the flood generation was characterized by active ungodliness; Sodom's inhabitants were defined by 'sensual conduct' and 'lawless deeds.' Noah was 'a preacher of righteousness'; Lot was 'righteous' and tormented by the wickedness around him. The division between eusebeis (godly) and asebeis (ungodly) is drawn along lines of conduct and character, not prior divine selection. The neutral reading does not indicate that the sinning angels were predestined to sin or that Noah was preserved by arbitrary decree apart from his righteousness. The passage implies that moral character -- which presupposes genuine agency -- is what distinguishes those God rescues from those God judges.
key_phrases: angels when they sinned
preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness
rescued righteous Lot
the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment

sections.section_title: The Recklessness of the False Teachers
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the false teachers are characterized as daring and self-willed, blaspheming angelic majesties without trembling, while even angels greater in power exercise restraint and defer to the Lord's authority in matters of judgment.

sections.section_title: The Nature and Behavior of the False Teachers
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the false teachers are compared to unreasoning animals and described as having hearts 'trained in greed,' with the neutral reading explicitly noting that their animal-like condition is 'not a description of human beings as God created them but of what these particular people have made themselves through their choices.'
sections.relevance: The neutral reading's comment that the false teachers 'have made themselves' into creatures of instinct through their choices directly bears on the determinism question. Their degraded condition is not attributed to divine decree or a nature imposed upon them, but to their own choices. Their hearts were 'trained' (gegymnasmenen -- exercised, disciplined) in greed, using the same language of deliberate cultivation that the author applied positively to the virtues in 1:5-7. They actively entice 'unstable souls' -- people whose salvific outcome is still undetermined and depends on whether they are lured away or become established.
key_phrases: what these particular people have made themselves through their choices
a heart trained in greed
enticing unstable souls
accursed children

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the false teachers are compared to Balaam, who knew God's word and spoke God's truth but was motivated by greed, and that the critical word 'forsaking' (kataleipontes) indicates these people 'were once on the right way' and 'did not start from outside; they departed from inside.'
sections.relevance: The Balaam typology reinforces human agency as the operative factor in departure from God. The neutral reading is explicit: 'These people were once on the right way. They did not start from outside; they departed from inside. The author does not say they never found the way, or that they only appeared to be on it. They were on the right way, and they left it.' The departure is described as a voluntary act of forsaking, not as a predetermined outcome. This bears on the determinism question because it presents the reversal of a genuine salvific relationship as the result of human choice.
key_phrases: forsaking the right way, they have gone astray
these people were once on the right way
they did not start from outside; they departed from inside
who loved the wages of unrighteousness

sections.section_title: The Emptiness of the False Teachers
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the false teachers are compared to springs without water and mists driven by a storm -- promising spiritual nourishment but offering nothing -- and that the 'black darkness' reserved for them echoes the confinement of the sinning angels in verse 4.

The neutral reading finds that the false teachers target 'those who barely escape from the ones who live in error' -- new converts in the vulnerable early stages of faith -- luring them back with sensuality while promising freedom, and states the universal principle: 'by what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved.'
sections.relevance: This passage directly addresses the mechanics of how salvation outcomes are determined, and it locates the mechanism in human agency on multiple levels. First, the false teachers' victims are people who are 'barely escaping' (oligos apopheugontas) -- their salvific outcome is genuinely in play, not yet determined. Second, the false teachers 'entice' them, implying the victims can be drawn back -- their escape is real but reversible through human response to temptation. Third, the principle 'by what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved' (v. 19) presents enslavement as the result of being overcome, which presupposes a contest in which the outcome is not predetermined. The author presents this as part of his core argument, not an illustration or aside.
key_phrases: those who barely escape from the ones who live in error
promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption
by what a man is overcome, by this he is enslaved
entice by fleshly desires

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that the author uses his strongest vocabulary for genuine spiritual experience -- the same words applied to the readers in chapter 1 -- to describe people who genuinely escaped the defilements of the world through knowledge of Christ, genuinely knew the way of righteousness, genuinely received the holy commandment, and then turned back, with the result that their last state is worse than the first.
sections.relevance: This is the chapter's climax and one of the most direct statements in the New Testament bearing on whether salvation outcomes are determined by God or by human agency. The neutral reading demonstrates that the author uses identical vocabulary (apophygontes, epignosis) for the false teachers' experience as for the readers' experience in chapter 1, without qualification or diminution. These people genuinely escaped; they genuinely knew. Their return to defilement was their own act: 'they are again entangled in them and are overcome.' The author's verdict -- 'the last state has become worse for them than the first' and 'it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than having known it, to turn away' -- presupposes that the turning away was a genuine human act that reversed a genuine salvific relationship. No divine decree is invoked to explain the reversal; no suggestion is made that these people were never truly purchased, never truly escaped, or never truly knew. The proverbs of v. 22 reinforce that the washing of the sow was real (lousamene) and the return to the mire was the sow's own act. The author makes this argument as the central thesis of the chapter, not as an aside.
key_phrases: after they have escaped the defilements of the world by the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ
they are again entangled in them and are overcome
the last state has become worse for them than the first
it would be better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than having known it, to turn away from the holy commandment
a sow, after washing, returns to wallowing in the mire
